This is somewhat hyperbolic. Sanders picked up 220 delegates to Hillary's 324. He now has 774 pledged delegates (eg - democratically voted) to Hillary's 1094, trailing by 320. He's still an underdog and became even more of an underdog after these recent results, but the race is hardly over. To put these numbers in contrast, California alone is worth 546 delegates.

The source you're reading from was likely including super delegates in the count. That certainly paints a far more grim pictures, but super delegates have never once gone against the popular vote - and in fact already turned sharply against Hillary in 2008 after supporting her last time once the popular vote swung to Obama. What remains to be seen is if Sanders can increase his support in the states to come to try to get those critical pledged delegates.

I'm aware that the super delegates could shift if Bernie somehow captures the popular vote. However, the midwest is probably one of the most friendly demographics for Bernie, primarily white working class people who are responsive to his message on trade. Not being able to take any of those states and getting decimated in Florida and North Carolina does not bode well. If not tonight, I'm not sure when the winds are supposed to suddenly change for him.

I think you have to look at things in terms of velocity to try to get an idea of what the future might hold. Even just a few weeks ago Sanders was losing most of these states by huge margins - 20, 30 points. In the end here 2 of the states were decided by 1 point. 2 were decent fights and then there was Florida which was a closed primary meaning only registered democrats could vote so Sanders, who relies on independents, never stood a chance.

I think the bigger problem for Sanders is not the numbers - the math is still fine, but momentum. The media, who wants Hillary in office, is going to trumpet a 5-0 huge sweeping victory for Clinton nonstop in what will be an effective attempt to demoralize Sanders supporters. Sanders is relying on grass roots funding. If this starts drying up, or his supporters stop showing up to the polls he could enter a rapid downward spiral.

On the other hand right now the only thing holding Clinton up is ignorance. She's scoring huge points on electability in spite of the fact that she scores substantially worse than Sanders in a general election against literally every single republican candidate. In fact she's losing against every republican except Trump whereas Sanders is winning against everybody!

Educating voters on the issues they're voting about is not easy, but he's continued to turn around from huge gaps so I think we still have an interesting race ahead where California may end up deciding everything.
It was a long uphill march against the super delegate system. I hope he prevails.
